name: DBMS & Operating Systems
description: Transactions, locking, processes, memory and the scheduling concepts interviewers expect you to connect.

modules.title: Transactions and Concurrency
content: ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Isolation is the property engines tune with isolation levels, and durability depends on write-ahead logging and fsync. Consistency is the least engine-specific of the four, because it names the invariants your application enforces, such as a balance that never goes negative, while the database only guarantees the constraints it knows about. Atomicity means a unit of work either lands wholly or not at all, so the engine must remember how to undo every change it made, which is why a logical batch split across two sessions can fail halfway and still leave committed data.

Two-phase locking has a growing phase that acquires locks and a shrinking phase that releases them. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit to avoid cascading aborts. Releasing a shared lock before commit is what lets another transaction overwrite a row you have already read, which is why strict implementations keep write locks to the end. The cost is throughput, because a long transaction holding one hot counter row can stall an entire service behind it, so lock views and engine status output turn an unexplained latency spike into a queue you can actually read.

Deadlocks can be prevented with ordering and timeouts, or detected with a wait-for graph whose victim transaction is rolled back. Ordering works only when every code path touches rows in the same sequence, and a loop over a user-selected set breaks that order silently. Timeouts are simpler and are what most engines ship, at the price of turning a contention spike into a spurious abort that the application must retry from the start of the unit of work rather than from the failing statement.

A transaction boundary also decides what a snapshot means, and vendors disagree about it. In PostgreSQL a transaction at Read Committed takes a fresh snapshot per statement, so a later statement can observe rows another transaction committed meanwhile, while at Repeatable Read the snapshot is fixed at the first statement and those commits stay invisible. MySQL and InnoDB behave differently again, because their default is Repeatable Read reinforced with next-key locking. Writing code against one vendor's snapshot semantics and deploying it on the other produces bugs that only appear under concurrency.

Engines expose shortcuts around the machinery, and each one quietly drops a guarantee you may still need. A read-only transaction can be served from a weaker snapshot and may take no row locks, so it cannot see your own uncommitted writes and can still block against a schema change. Long-running transactions look harmless but pin row versions: in PostgreSQL vacuum cannot recycle dead tuples a live snapshot still needs, so tables bloat, and in InnoDB the history list grows and every writer pays for the cleanup eventually.

Atomic commit across several resources needs more than local undo logs. Two-phase commit has a coordinator ask each participant to prepare, which means flushing its log to durable storage and voting, after which the coordinator records its own decision and tells everyone to commit. The blocking property is the painful part: a participant that has prepared cannot back out, so if the coordinator dies its rows stay locked until it recovers. That is why a single service transaction should map to one database, and why cross-database updates become sagas with compensating actions instead.

Autocommit wraps every statement in its own transaction, so a multi-statement update that should be atomic is applied in pieces and an error halfway leaves the database perfectly consistent and completely wrong. Frameworks hide this well: a session opened outside the ORM transaction manager, a raw pooled connection left in autocommit, or DDL that some engines commit implicitly all silently widen the boundary. Debugging a concurrency report therefore starts by logging when the transaction really began and committed, not by reading the SQL text.

modules.title: Processes, Memory and Scheduling
content: A process has its own virtual address space; threads within it share that space and file descriptors while keeping separate stacks and registers. Sharing is what makes threads cheap and dangerous at once, because a race on a shared map corrupts state no compiler warning catches, and one thread that closes a socket or blocks a signal affects all its siblings. Isolation between processes costs a page-table copy on creation and forces communication through pipes or shared memory, which is why many servers run a small process pool with a few threads per worker.

A page fault means the referenced page is not resident, so the kernel loads it from disk or swap. Excessive faulting produces thrashing, where the system spends most time paging. The handler has to find a free frame, possibly evict a victim, update the page tables and restart the faulting instruction, so the cost is microseconds to milliseconds rather than nanoseconds. Thrashing is a workload-level failure rather than a scheduling one, and the cure is fewer resident jobs or more memory, which is what working-set models and the page-out daemon try to approximate.

Round-robin scheduling gives each runnable process a fixed time slice, improving responsiveness at the cost of context-switch overhead. Picking the quantum is the whole design problem: a slice far longer than the switch cost keeps throughput high but makes interactive latency jittery, while a tiny slice turns the processor into overhead management. Real schedulers refine rotation into proportional share, as with the Linux Completely Fair Scheduler's virtual runtime accounting, per-core run queues and sleeper awareness.

Creating a task on Unix is a two-step dance: fork duplicates the address space lazily through copy-on-write, then exec throws that copy away and installs a new program image. The consequence is that a program which forks many children without exec can exhaust the process id space and memory, and that fork of a large process is cheap only until the children start writing. Threads are created by clone-style syscalls that share the memory mappings, file table and signal handlers while giving each its own stack, which is why stack limits are per thread.

Schedulers are judged by what they optimise, and the metrics fight each other. Turnaround time rewards long batch jobs, response time rewards short interactive ones, and fairness penalises a bursty process that keeps getting postponed. Preemption makes response time possible but depends on the timer interrupt and on kernel code returning promptly, so a section that holds a spinlock with interrupts disabled produces latency spikes no userspace tuning can fix. Measuring wakeup-to-running delay is how you find those sections.

Priority scheduling fails in a subtle way when a high-priority task blocks on a lock held by a low-priority one that medium-priority tasks keep outrunning: the high-priority job effectively waits for the least urgent thread, which is priority inversion, and it once forced an in-flight fix on a Mars mission. Unbounded inversion is prevented by inheriting the holder's priority, by a priority ceiling, or simply by aging a waiting task until it runs. Nice values only shift weight inside one scheduling class; they do not make a busy loop yield to a kernel thread.

Each process sees a private address space split into text, initialised and uninitialised data, a heap that grows through brk or mmap, and a stack with a guard page so runaway recursion becomes a fault instead of silent corruption. Shared libraries are mapped from the page cache into every process, so a library's text costs physical memory once however many processes use it. Overcommit decides whether malloc may return a pointer the kernel cannot later back with a frame, and the Linux default happily overpromises until the out-of-memory killer picks a victim.

modules.title: Isolation Levels and Read Anomalies
content: The SQL standard defines four levels by the anomalies they must forbid: Read Uncommitted permits dirty reads, Read Committed forbids those but allows non-repeatable reads, Repeatable Read forbids those but allows phantoms, and Serializable forbids all three. The definition is written as a short list of symptoms rather than as a positive guarantee, which is why a level can pass every test the standard names and still feel wrong: it never states what a transaction is allowed to see, only what it must not.

A dirty read is reading data another transaction has not committed yet, so the value may vanish when that transaction rolls back. A non-repeatable read is reading one row twice in a transaction and getting different values because someone updated it in between. A phantom read is re-running a range predicate and finding rows that appeared or disappeared because of inserts or deletes. Phantoms differ because the result set changes size instead of a value changing, which is why preventing them needs predicate or gap locking rather than row locking alone.

Beyond the standard's list sit the anomalies that bite teams running at Read Committed. A lost update happens when two transactions read a counter and each writes back the value it read plus one, so an increment disappears; engines fix it with an atomic statement or a locking read. Write skew is subtler: each transaction reads a set of rows, then updates a different row based on what it did not see, so both commits are individually valid and jointly wrong. Only serializability, or snapshot isolation with write-serialization checks, reliably rejects it.

PostgreSQL implements Read Uncommitted as an alias for Read Committed with a warning, because dirty reads are incompatible with how it stores versions. It offers Read Committed as the default, then Repeatable Read and Serializable, where the last two are true snapshot isolation rather than the standard's weaker readings. At Serializable the engine tracks read and write dependencies and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001 when a cycle forms, so retry logic is mandatory. The default therefore permits both non-repeatable reads and phantoms, and code that assumes one stable view of a table across statements needs a higher level.

InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read and prevents phantoms inside a transaction with next-key locking, a combination of a row lock and a gap lock that blocks inserts into the range an earlier query scanned. That is stronger than the standard's Repeatable Read, and the practical consequence is that a locking read over a range can lock rows that do not exist yet. InnoDB still permits a write-skew shape through snapshot reads, because a plain SELECT takes no lock, while an UPDATE re-reads the latest committed version, so the operational rule is to use a locking read whenever the read is a guard for a write.

Higher levels cost measurable money. Serializable aborts a real fraction of concurrent write-heavy workloads, so systems either retry transparently or funnel conflicting writes through one worker. Repeatable Read pins a snapshot for the whole transaction, which increases version cleanup and bloat. Read Committed re-reads per statement and surprises developers who assumed the transaction saw a single moment. Picking a level means predicting your actual interference pattern, and the honest answer comes from running the real access pattern concurrently rather than from a table in a tutorial.

MVCC lets readers proceed without blocking writers, and that is exactly why an unlocked SELECT cannot serve as a guard for an UPDATE: the check reads a past version while the write lands on the current one. A locking read re-evaluates against the latest committed row and holds it, and variants that skip locked rows let queue consumers take work without piling into a lock queue. Most real-world double-processing and double-booking bugs are this one gap, not a missing index or a slow query.

modules.title: Virtual Memory, Paging and TLB
content: Paging divides virtual and physical memory into fixed-size blocks, usually four kilobytes, so the kernel can back any virtual page with any free frame and never needs contiguous physical memory. A page table maps virtual to physical through a multi-level structure whose leaf holds the frame number plus permission, dirty and referenced bits. External fragmentation stops being a scheduling problem because any frame fits, and the only remaining waste is the unused tail of the last page of an allocation, which is why many small allocations still cost a page each.

Translating every memory reference through the page table would multiply latency, so the processor caches translations in a translation lookaside buffer. A TLB miss is worse than a cache miss because the hardware may walk several page-table levels, with a cache miss at each step, unless a dedicated walker shortcuts it. Any mapping change requires a flush, and process switches either invalidate entries or use address-space tags, which is why a context switch is not merely register save and restore but also a cold TLB for the incoming task.

Huge pages of two megabytes or a gigabyte shrink the walk depth and let one TLB entry cover far more memory, which is why databases and large heaps request them explicitly. Automatic huge pages deliver the same hit-rate gain but can hurt latency-sensitive workloads, because allocation may trigger synchronous memory compaction and because copy-on-write of a huge page copies the whole two megabytes when a single byte is touched. The usual tuning outcome is to keep the explicit pool and disable the speculative defragmenter rather than accept unpredictable stalls.

When memory runs out, the kernel must choose a victim page, and exact least-recently-used tracking is too expensive, so it approximates. Linux keeps active and inactive lists and uses the referenced bit plus periodic scanning to promote and demote pages, with the second-chance clock as the textbook shape. The cost model matters more than the algorithm name: evicting a clean file page just drops it, while evicting a dirty page means writing it back first, so a cache eviction storm becomes disk traffic that shows up as latency everywhere else.

Programs do not touch memory uniformly; they cluster in a working set, and locality is what makes caches and prefetching profitable. It is also what makes capacity behave oddly: a set of jobs each just under the available memory runs fine until one grows, at which point everybody starts faulting for the same frames. Both the working-set and local-time models say the same operational thing, that the number of resident jobs must adapt to demand, which is why the kernel swaps out idle pages instead of letting one allocation push the machine into thrashing.

Swap is an emergency extension of memory, not a slow disk for the heap. Because a page has to be dirty to be worth evicting, read-only program text never lands in swap; it is simply re-read from the file, which is why watching total swap usage misleads people who expect it to mirror heap pressure. When reclaim cannot find frames, the out-of-memory killer scores processes by memory usage plus a few heuristics and terminates one, so an overcommitted workload dies with an unexplained signal while the kernel log quietly explains it.

Demand paging maps pages lazily, so the first touch of a freshly mapped region costs a minor fault; a program that allocates gigabytes and then writes all of them pays for that page by page, which is why some servers pre-touch memory at startup to move the cost out of the request path. Locking a region pins it against eviction, which is right for key material and real-time loops and dangerous in bulk, because pinning too much leaves the machine nothing to reclaim. Aligning allocations and touching memory in dense bursts reduces both fault counts and TLB pressure.

modules.title: Write-Ahead Logging and Crash Recovery
content: The write-ahead protocol says a change is not applied to a data file until the record describing it is durable in the log. Log records are appended sequentially, so durability costs one sequential write instead of many random page writes, and the log becomes the single authority about what was intended. The page itself can then be flushed lazily by a background writer, which is what turns a burst of commits into an amortised trickle of random I/O and keeps commit latency roughly independent of how much data the transaction touched.

Every log record carries a monotonically increasing log sequence number, and each data page remembers the number of the last change applied to it. The two ordering rules that follow are essentially the whole algorithm: before a page is written, the log up to that page's number must be durable, and before a commit is acknowledged, the commit record and everything before it must be durable. Violating either produces a page that asserts a change no log admits, which recovery cannot distinguish from physical corruption.

Redo logging stores the new value so a change can be replayed; undo logging stores the old value so an unfinished transaction can be rolled back. Most engines log both, and reduce logical operations to physical byte writes so that redo is idempotent, which is what makes it safe to run the recovery pass twice after a crash during recovery. Logging every modified byte is boring but robust; logical logging produces a smaller stream that replays faster, provided every operation is written so its effect is either fully applied or cleanly repeated.

Recovery runs as analysis, redo and undo. Analysis reads the log from the last checkpoint to rebuild which transactions were active and which pages were dirty at the crash. Redo then repeats history from that point, applying every logged change whether it eventually committed or not, because the in-memory image must be brought to the newest state the log describes before anything can be undone. Undo rolls back the transactions that never committed, logging its own progress through undo-next pointers so an interrupted rollback is resumable. Skipping or shortening the redo pass is how a recovery turns a database into rubble.

Checkpointing bounds recovery time by recording where the log's durable state and the dirty-page set agree, and fuzzy or steady checkpoints do it by forcing pages gradually so the log head keeps advancing. Without checkpoints the log can never be recycled and recovery replays years of records; with aggressive ones, the write bursts at each checkpoint produce the sawtooth latency profile operators learn to recognise. Engines therefore expose checkpoint interval and log size as paired knobs, because there is no configuration that bounds both recovery time and write spikes for free.

A write that returns success is not the same as a durable write. The operating system absorbs writes into the page cache, and drives with volatile write caches acknowledge before the media holds the bytes, so a power loss can lose data the application was told was safe. Engines ask for flushes and barriers, and on some filesystems need mount options that disable delayed allocation, or drive caches disabled entirely, to get the promise. Group commit amortises the price by letting several transactions share one flush, which is why commit throughput can rise when you add load.

Corruption usually arrives through the assumptions around the log rather than the log itself. A directory copied while the server writes produces pages and a log captured from different instants, and recovery will faithfully replay committed changes onto the wrong base. Truncating or deleting a log segment to free disk space converts an ordinary crash into an unrecoverable state. A network filesystem that does not implement barriers honestly breaks the durability contract, which is why engines forbid shared local-filesystem storage and require replication instead.

modules.title: File Systems, Caching and I/O Paths
content: A filesystem sits between the virtual layer that gives read and write one uniform shape across local and network storage, and the block layer that schedules requests for the device. An extent-based journal records metadata changes so a crash leaves either a complete update or none, rather than a half-linked directory. File data is journalled only if you ask for it, and ordered mode sits between by forcing data blocks out before the metadata that references them, which is why a rename survives a crash while the new content of the file may not.

Linux caches file contents in the page cache, shared between processes, so the second read of a block costs memory speed instead of device time. Readahead speculates that a sequential pattern will continue and fetches ahead, which roughly doubles streaming throughput and roughly halves it for random access patterns such as a database walking its own pages, because the kernel fetches data nobody requested and evicts useful pages to make room. That speculation is the main reason databases bypass the cache and manage residency themselves.

Writes land in the page cache as dirty and are flushed later by background writeback according to age and dirty-ratio thresholds. That is excellent for throughput and useless for durability, so a synchronous flush forces one file's dirty data and the metadata describing it down to the device, sometimes dragging unrelated dirty data along with it. When the dirty limits are reached the kernel throttles writers by making them write pages themselves, so a burst of large file copies can stall an unrelated process inside a plain write call.

Writing a file in place can leave a truncated version if power is lost halfway, which is why the standard trick for replacing a file is to write a temporary one and rename it, since renaming a directory entry is a single metadata operation. Getting that right requires a durability flush on the new file and then another on the containing directory, because the directory entry is what makes the rename itself durable; skipping the second sync gives files that exist after boot with the old contents. Access-time updates add write traffic for almost no benefit, which is why relatime and noatime are near-universal defaults.

Rotating disks made seek order matter, which is why deadline and proportional-share schedulers exist and why a log device was once worth separating onto its own spindle. Flash removes the seek penalty but adds write amplification, because the translation layer rewrites whole erase blocks to service small random overwrites, so an untrimmed device slows down as it fills and a queue depth too low cannot exploit the parallelism inside it. Modern interfaces expose many submission queues precisely so many cores can submit without contending on one lock.

Two caches in a stack are usually a mistake: an application buffer above the page cache means data is copied twice and evicted twice, and the two eviction policies fight. Direct I/O bypasses the page cache, at the price of alignment requirements and losing shared caching, readahead and cheap small writes, and it gives the application full responsibility for what stays resident. The same confusion shows up in containers, where cache that looks like committed memory can be reclaimed instantly, so a limit that appears unused is often exactly what is keeping a workload alive.

Mount and journal settings decide what durability you actually receive. A filesystem that delays allocations for several seconds can lose acknowledged data on a crash, and ordered mode plus shorter intervals or direct I/O are the mitigations. Network filesystems cache attributes, so a file written by one client can look unchanged to another until the cache expires. A layered container filesystem copies a file up before the first write, which surprises anything appending to a large log. Each of these is invisible until it is the root cause of the data you lost.

modules.title: Buffer Pools, Storage Engines and Checkpointing
content: A buffer pool is the database's own cache of fixed-size pages, managed by a clock-style approximation with pin counts so a page cannot be evicted while a cursor stands on it. It exists because the operating system cache does not know which pages the next query needs, when a page must be forced to satisfy log ordering, or which page is dirty for how long. Since both caches compete for the same RAM, the practical sizing rule is to leave the kernel very little and to give the pool memory that the working set can actually fill.

Pool hit rate is measured per page access, not per query, and a nominal 95 percent can still be catastrophic if the missing five percent are the ones on the critical path of a millisecond-latency service. Sizing the pool far beyond the hot set wastes memory that other processes need, lengthens the flush backlog, and delays log recycling, so the correct target is the working set rather than available RAM. Growth and shrink policies matter too, because a pool that never releases pages turns an OLTP table's bulk load into permanent memory loss for the rest of the box.

InnoDB stores a table as a clustered B+tree whose leaf pages hold full rows in primary-key order, so a key lookup is one descent and a range scan is sequential at the leaf level. Secondary indexes store the key plus the primary key, so matching them requires a second descent to fetch the row, which is why a covering index changes the cost so dramatically. A wide or random primary key inflates every secondary index and scatters inserts across the tree, producing page splits everywhere instead of appending to the right edge.

An LSM tree inverts that trade-off: writes append to a mutable table, become immutable, and are flushed as sorted runs that a background compactor merges into larger levels. Insertions are nearly free and sequential, which suits log-like and ingest-heavy workloads, but a read may consult several levels before a bloom filter can prove absence, and compaction steals I/O and CPU in bursts. Tuning such an engine mostly means choosing level ratios and compaction concurrency, and the same settings behave like two different products on a hard disk and on a flash device.

Row versioning means an update creates a new version rather than overwriting, and somebody has to collect the garbage. InnoDB keeps undo records and purges versions older than the oldest active read view; PostgreSQL marks tuples dead and relies on an autovacuum process to reclaim space in place. Both fail the same way: one idle-in-transaction session pins the cleanup horizon, dead versions accumulate, tables and indexes bloat, and plans degrade as statistics drift. Bloat is therefore a session-hygiene symptom, not evidence that the storage format is wrong.

Fuzzy checkpointing lets dirty pages linger so write work spreads out, but the log constrains how long they may linger: once the oldest dirty page is too far behind the log head, the engine cannot recycle the log and stalls writers until flushing catches up, which is what a sudden throughput cliff looks like. Doublewrite buffering exists because a page write can be torn by a crash when the device's atomic unit is smaller than the page, and the engine keeps a copy to restore from. Disabling it to buy throughput is a corruption gamble.

Pluggable storage makes the engine choice per table, and the failure modes differ visibly. Column-oriented layouts compress well and scan a few columns fast but pay to reassemble rows on update-heavy tables. Compression saves I/O and pool space, and on modern CPUs decompression is cheaper than the read it avoids, but it makes each page self-contained so a torn page is unusable without the extra copy. Choosing an engine from a benchmark rather than from your update pattern is how a team ends up with a fast test and a slow production table.

modules.title: Synchronization, Deadlocks and Liveness
content: A mutex grants exclusive ownership to one thread and expects that same thread to release it; a counting semaphore grants N permits and has no owner, so any thread may signal it. The distinction drives real behaviour, because ownership enables priority inheritance and error checks such as releasing a lock you do not hold, while a semaphore is the natural fit for a resource pool or a producer-consumer count. A binary semaphore can implement mutual exclusion but does so without any of those protections, which is why it is the usual source of wake-ups nobody can explain.

Locking inside a kernel means spinning, because the holder may be running on another core and sleeping would be slower than waiting. A spinlock therefore guards short, non-blocking sections and disables preemption so the holder cannot be postponed while others spin; sleeping locks allow the caller to block instead. Calling something that may sleep while holding a spinlock is a bug the kernel can catch with debug options, and the symptom of getting it wrong in a driver is random watchdog panics that only appear under load.

Atomic operations are not merely indivisible, because without ordering the compiler and the processor may move other accesses around them. Memory models split this into relaxed, acquire, release and sequentially consistent operations, and the correct publication pattern is release on the writer and acquire on the reader, which is what makes a pointer or a queue slot safe to hand over. Dekker-style algorithms fail on weakly ordered hardware without a fence, which explains why lock-free code tested only on x86 can break on architectures with a much more relaxed order.

Deadlock requires four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Breaking any single one suffices, and the standard techniques map directly onto them: a global lock order kills circular wait, try-lock with backoff kills hold-and-wait, a timeout converts deadlock into an error, and packing the state into one atomic word removes the need for multiple locks at all. Wait-for graphs suit databases because aborting a victim is cheap, whereas in an operating system a killed process may have already produced external effects, so detection leaves you choosing a mess rather than a clean undo.

Liveness failures are broader than deadlock. Starvation is a scheduling or lock policy that keeps postponing one task indefinitely. Livelock is threads that make logical progress but never forward, like two people dodging the same way, and it shows up in retry loops that wake on the same timer, which randomised backoff fixes. The convoy effect happens when a long critical section queues a group of waiters that then serialise behind each other on release and block the next arrivals, producing stair-step throughput; queued fairness and shorter sections are the cure.

Condition variables deliberately separate waiting from locking: you hold the mutex, test the predicate in a loop, then wait, which atomically releases the mutex and blocks. The loop is mandatory because wake-ups can be spurious and because another thread can consume the state between the signal and your reschedule, so a single if-test is a bug that hides until load. Signalling while holding the lock hands ownership directly but causes an immediate fight for it, and broadcasting wakes every waiter when only one can proceed, which is a thundering herd by construction.

Kernel and database locking meet in the middle and both fail without care. Readers-writer locks let many readers proceed but can starve writers, so queued variants alternate; a seqlock lets writers always win and makes readers retry if they observed a torn write. In databases, advisory locks coordinate application work without touching rows, and a row lock held across a network call becomes a service-wide outage when that call stalls. Any lock whose hold time depends on the network needs a timeout, and any timeout needs a retry budget.

questions.text: What does ACID stand for?
questions.a: Availability, Consistency, Integrity, Durability
questions.b: Atomicity, Concurrency, Isolation, Distribution
questions.c: Accuracy, Consistency, Isolation, Dependency
questions.d: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
questions.explanation: Each property addresses a distinct failure mode: partial commits, invariants, concurrent interference and crashes.

questions.text: What are the phases of two-phase locking?
questions.a: Locks are released immediately after each read
questions.b: It prevents deadlocks through timestamp ordering
questions.c: Growing phase acquires locks; shrinking phase releases them
questions.d: It requires optimistic validation
questions.explanation: No lock may be acquired after the first release, which guarantees serializability.

questions.text: How do database systems handle deadlocks?
questions.a: Deadlocks cannot occur between transactions
questions.b: Detection aborts a victim; prevention uses ordering or timeouts
questions.c: The DBMS waits forever
questions.d: READ COMMITTED prevents all deadlocks because it releases locks early
questions.explanation: A wait-for cycle means no transaction can proceed, so one is chosen as the victim and rolled back.

questions.text: What is the key memory difference between processes and threads?
questions.a: Threads of one process share the address space; processes are isolated
questions.b: Processes share memory by default
questions.c: Threads cannot share file descriptors because each thread has its own table
questions.d: A process cannot contain multiple threads
questions.explanation: Isolation makes processes safer but costlier to create and communicate between; threads share memory and must synchronize.

questions.text: What does a page fault indicate?
questions.a: The process has terminated
questions.b: The disk is full
questions.c: Swap is disabled, so every page fault immediately becomes a fatal error
questions.d: The referenced page is not in physical memory and must be brought in
questions.explanation: A minor fault may be satisfied from the page cache; a major fault requires disk I/O.

questions.text: What happens during a context switch?
questions.a: The kernel saves the current task state and restores the next task
questions.b: The entire heap is copied
questions.c: No overhead is incurred
questions.d: It only happens on multi-core systems
questions.explanation: Registers, program counter and stack pointer are saved and restored, which is why excessive switching hurts throughput.

questions.text: How does a mutex differ from a counting semaphore?
questions.a: They are identical
questions.b: A semaphore cannot provide mutual exclusion
questions.c: A mutex has no owner, so any thread can release it at any time
questions.d: A mutex is an owned binary lock; a semaphore allows N permits
questions.explanation: Ownership lets a mutex support priority inheritance and recursive locking; semaphores are counters without ownership.

questions.text: What is thrashing?
questions.a: A CPU scheduling algorithm
questions.b: High CPU utilization with no paging activity or disk I/O at all
questions.c: Excessive paging leaves little time for useful work
questions.d: A deadlock between two threads
questions.explanation: When the working set exceeds physical memory, the system swaps pages in and out continuously and throughput collapses.

questions.text: How does round-robin scheduling work?
questions.a: Each process runs to completion
questions.b: It starves short jobs because long jobs always run to completion each time
questions.c: Processes get a fixed time slice in rotation, improving responsiveness
questions.d: It requires priority aging
questions.explanation: Each runnable process gets a quantum in turn, which bounds waiting time for interactive work.

questions.text: Why do filesystems use journaling?
questions.a: Journals encrypt every file
questions.b: Journals log metadata for crash recovery
questions.c: Journals replace backups
questions.d: Journals are only used by database systems
questions.explanation: Replaying or discarding an incomplete journal entry avoids scanning the entire disk and prevents corrupt metadata.

questions.text: What must happen before a dirty page may be written to the data file?
questions.a: The log records describing that page change must be durable
questions.b: The page must be moved to the buffer pool free list first
questions.c: Every transaction that touched it must already have committed
questions.d: The checkpoint record must be appended after the page write
questions.explanation: Write-ahead ordering is log-before-data, so the intent survives even if the page write is lost. Option D inverts the order, which is exactly the violation recovery cannot repair.

questions.text: In ARIES recovery, why does the redo phase replay changes made by transactions that later aborted?
questions.a: Undo always runs before redo, so redo only has to visit aborted transactions
questions.b: Redo rebuilds the newest logged state before undo removes uncommitted work
questions.c: Aborted transactions never emit undo records in the log at all
questions.d: Redo can be skipped when the last checkpoint was very recent
questions.explanation: Recovery must first repeat history to the newest logged page image, then roll back what never committed. Option A reverses the two passes, which is the classic misremembering of ARIES order.

questions.text: Which anomaly is possible at Read Committed but prevented at Repeatable Read?
questions.a: Reading another transaction's uncommitted row
questions.b: A lost update avoided by an atomic increment statement
questions.c: Re-reading the same row and getting a different value
questions.d: A sequential scan chosen instead of an index scan
questions.explanation: That is the non-repeatable read the level is named for. Option A is already forbidden at Read Committed, so it is one rung too low on the ladder.

questions.text: Under PostgreSQL's Serializable isolation, what makes a transaction abort with a serialization failure?
questions.a: It waited longer than lock_timeout on a row held by another session
questions.b: Vacuum removed a row version its snapshot still needed
questions.c: Another session ran a DDL statement on the same table
questions.d: The engine found a dependency cycle among concurrent transactions
questions.explanation: Serializable snapshot isolation aborts only when dependency cycles prove a non-serializable interleaving. Option A is a plain lock timeout, a different error that no isolation level causes.

questions.text: What does a checkpoint primarily buy a logging database?
questions.a: It permanently shrinks the data files on disk
questions.b: It bounds recovery time so earlier log can be recycled
questions.c: It guarantees that no transaction is ever rolled back
questions.d: It removes the need for any write-ahead logging at commit time
questions.explanation: A checkpoint marks a point from which recovery can start, freeing the log before it. Option A confuses checkpointing with vacuum or compaction, which reclaim space rather than time.

questions.text: Why should a read that guards an UPDATE be a locking read rather than a plain one under MVCC?
questions.a: A locking read sees the latest version; a snapshot read may test an old one
questions.b: A plain SELECT takes an exclusive lock on every row the scan touches and keeps it
questions.c: A locking read skips write-ahead logging for that statement
questions.d: MVCC guarantees two transactions never update the same row
questions.explanation: Readers see a version, writers modify the current one, so an unlocked guard is checked against the past. Option B states the opposite of how MVCC readers behave.

questions.text: What is write skew?
questions.a: Two transactions lock exactly the same rows in the opposite order and then block forever
questions.b: One transaction reads another's uncommitted writes
questions.c: Each transaction updates a different row based on a stale read of the same set
questions.d: A page flushed to disk before its log record reaches it
questions.explanation: Both commits are individually valid and jointly wrong, which plain read-only conflict detection misses. Option A describes a deadlock, not an isolation anomaly.

questions.text: Why is a long-running read-only transaction harmful in PostgreSQL?
questions.a: It forces every other reader into its lock queue
questions.b: It pins dead row versions so vacuum cannot reclaim them
questions.c: It silently upgrades every scanned table to serializable predicate locking
questions.d: It disables least-recently-used eviction in the pool
questions.explanation: The snapshot defines the cleanup horizon, so dead tuples and their indexes accumulate. Option A is wrong because MVCC readers do not block one another.

questions.text: In two-phase commit, what happens if the coordinator crashes after participants have prepared?
questions.a: Each participant rolls back at once and releases every lock it still holds
questions.b: Recovery replays every participant's log independently
questions.c: The application simply reissues the prepared records
questions.d: Participants block and keep locks until the coordinator recovers
questions.explanation: Prepared is the point of no return, so a participant can neither commit nor abort alone. Option A sounds safe but would break atomicity if one participant had already committed.

questions.text: Which statement about fsync and durability is correct?
questions.a: A completed write reaches the cache; fsync asks for the device
questions.b: Disks never cache writes, so fsync is a formality
questions.c: Syncing a file necessarily syncs every entry in its parent directory as well
questions.d: Group commit removes the need to flush the log at all
questions.explanation: The page cache and volatile drive caches absorb writes until an explicit flush. Option C is the trap that bites rename-based writers: the directory entry needs its own sync.

questions.text: What does an undo log make possible?
questions.a: Faster index lookups by keeping every key in sorted leaf order
questions.b: Durable commits without any log flushing
questions.c: Rolling a transaction's changes back to its start
questions.d: Automatic parallelism across CPU cores
questions.explanation: Undo records hold old values so atomicity survives a mid-transaction failure. Option B confuses undo with the redo-plus-fsync path that provides durability.

questions.text: Why does an engine keep its own buffer pool instead of trusting the kernel page cache?
questions.a: The kernel page cache cannot hold more than one gigabyte of file data
questions.b: The engine needs control over forcing and eviction choice
questions.c: Kernel frames cannot be mapped into user space
questions.d: A pool removes the need to ever read from disk
questions.explanation: Log ordering requires forcing a specific page, and query plans hint at which pages stay hot. Option D mistakes a cache for a guarantee; cold pages still must be read.

questions.text: What problem does a doublewrite buffer solve?
questions.a: It duplicates the log so a corrupt segment can be skipped
questions.b: It keeps two independent copies of every index so that a crash is survivable
questions.c: It repairs partially written pages when the device writes smaller units
questions.d: It speeds range scans by prefetching sibling pages
questions.explanation: When a page write is torn by a crash, the checksum cannot identify which bytes are valid, so a private copy restores it. Option A confuses it with log archiving.

questions.text: How does a clustered index shape secondary index lookups?
questions.a: Secondary indexes hold the primary key, so a hit needs a second descent
questions.b: Secondary indexes hold row offsets, so any update invalidates them
questions.c: Secondary indexes hold a complete copy of every row, so no lookup is added
questions.d: The clustered tree is rebuilt whenever a secondary index is used
questions.explanation: The leaf of a secondary entry is a key pointer, requiring another B+tree walk to fetch the row. Option C describes a covering index, which is the special case, not the rule.

questions.text: What distinguishes an LSM tree's read path from a B+tree's?
questions.a: An LSM read touches exactly one sorted run on storage
questions.b: An LSM read is always cheaper because compaction is synchronous
questions.c: An LSM read needs no bloom filter since keys are hashed
questions.d: An LSM read may check a memtable plus several levels of files
questions.explanation: Newest data lives in memory and older data is spread over levels, so reads fan out. Option C inverts it: bloom filters exist precisely to prune those levels cheaply.

questions.text: What does it mean when a database reports that a commit succeeded?
questions.a: Every page it touched is now written to the data files
questions.b: The transaction's log records are durable on storage
questions.c: All replicas applied it before the acknowledgement
questions.d: Its locks have already been handed to waiting sessions
questions.explanation: Durability is defined on the log, and data pages are flushed later. Option A is the intuitive but wrong reading, since the background writer still owes the disk.

questions.text: Why can checkpoint age throttle write throughput?
questions.a: Checkpoints compress the log, so writers wait on the compressor thread
questions.b: A checkpoint deletes old data pages as it progresses
questions.c: Dirty pages must be flushed before the log can be reused
questions.d: A checkpoint takes an exclusive lock on every table
questions.explanation: Log space can only be recycled past the oldest dirty page, so lagging flushes stall writers. Option D confuses fuzzy checkpointing with a stop-the-world flush.

questions.text: A data directory is copied while the server keeps writing, with the log captured at a different instant. Why is the copy unsafe?
questions.a: Recovery may replay logged changes onto pages from another point in time
questions.b: The log format version changes as soon as a write occurs
questions.c: Page checksums are only recomputed at a clean shutdown
questions.d: The kernel refuses to copy files that are open for writing at that moment
questions.explanation: Write-ahead correctness assumes log and pages came from one consistent moment. Option D is a real operational nuisance for some tools, but it is not why the copy is corrupt.

questions.text: What do gap locks in InnoDB protect against?
questions.a: Long transactions that hold undo segments for far too brief a period
questions.b: Dirty pages being flushed ahead of their log records
questions.c: Deadlocks between two writers updating the same row
questions.d: Inserts into a range an earlier read in the transaction scanned
questions.explanation: Locking the empty space between keys is what stops phantoms under Repeatable Read. Option C confuses them with ordinary row locks, which gap locking does not remove.

questions.text: What is an advisory lock in a relational database for?
questions.a: Warning the query optimiser that a cached plan has become unstable
questions.b: Forcing vacuum to run on one specific table
questions.c: Coordinating sessions without locking any table rows
questions.d: Logging statements slower than a threshold
questions.explanation: Applications claim named keys to serialise work such as cron runs or queue leases. Option B confuses it with maintenance tooling that operates on real relation metadata.

questions.text: Two transactions each hold one row lock and wait for the other. How do PostgreSQL and InnoDB respond?
questions.a: Both detect the cycle and abort a victim, with different tuning
questions.b: Only InnoDB detects cycles, while PostgreSQL has no detector at all
questions.c: Neither detects it, so both wait for a client to disconnect
questions.d: Both kill the session and undo its committed work too
questions.explanation: Each ships a deadlock detector with a probe delay, so the difference is in thresholds and messages. Option B is a common half-truth about the older PostgreSQL behaviour.

questions.text: What does the log sequence number stored on a data page record?
questions.a: How many times the page was read since startup
questions.b: The last logged change applied to that page
questions.c: The identifier of the transaction that created the page
questions.d: The count of free slots in the page directory
questions.explanation: It is the watermark that lets recovery decide whether a page already contains a logged change. Option C is tempting because logs do carry transaction ids, but the page stores position, not authorship.

questions.text: Why is purely logical redo logging risky for a recovery pass?
questions.a: Logical redo records cannot be written concurrently with ordinary DML statements
questions.b: Logical records make checkpoint scheduling impossible
questions.c: They force the undo phase to run before the redo phase
questions.d: Replay must reproduce the effect exactly, which byte copies do for free
questions.explanation: An operation that references row versions, statistics or ordering may not replay to the same result, so idempotence has to be engineered. Option C mistakes a logging format choice for a pass ordering.

questions.text: What is a transaction in database terms?
questions.a: Any single SELECT statement issued by a client
questions.b: A sequence of operations treated as one indivisible unit of work
questions.c: The time a query spends queued behind a lock before it can execute
questions.d: A request that the server executes without any logging
questions.explanation: The unit boundary is what atomicity and isolation are applied to. Option A is only a degenerate case, because autocommit makes each statement its own unit.

questions.text: What does copy-on-write make fork inexpensive?
questions.a: It defers duplicating the parent's file descriptor table
questions.b: It skips creating a page table for the child
questions.c: It avoids copying any page until one side writes it
questions.d: It shares the parent's stack for the child's first frames
questions.explanation: Writable mappings are marked read-only in both copies and duplicated on the first store. Option A is wrong because the descriptor table and signal state are duplicated eagerly.

questions.text: Why is a TLB miss often costlier than a data cache miss?
questions.a: The TLB stores decompressed page contents rather than translations
questions.b: The walk may touch several page-table levels, each missing cache
questions.c: TLB entries are invalidated by every timer interrupt
questions.d: Huge pages are never entered into the TLB at all
questions.explanation: A multi-level walk can turn one translation into a chain of dependent memory accesses. Option D is false; huge pages actually improve TLB coverage dramatically.

questions.text: What does the Linux swappiness setting express?
questions.a: The maximum swap partition size in megabytes
questions.b: How quickly the OOM killer scores candidate processes under pressure
questions.c: How often a thread migrates between CPU cores
questions.d: How eagerly reclaim prefers page cache over anonymous pages
questions.explanation: It biases the victim choice between dropping file pages and swapping out process memory. Option B confuses it with the separately computed badness score used at OOM time.

questions.text: What separates a minor from a major page fault?
questions.a: A minor is served from memory already present; a major needs I/O
questions.b: A minor is raised by the kernel, a major by user space
questions.c: A minor fault never blocks the faulting process under any circumstances
questions.d: A major fault can only occur on memory-mapped files
questions.explanation: The distinction is whether a disk or swap read is required. Option C is the trap, since a minor fault still suspends the thread while the handler runs.

questions.text: Why can automatic huge pages raise latency for a workload that forks a large process?
questions.a: Huge pages cannot be swapped, so memory use only grows
questions.b: They turn off the TLB on most modern processors
questions.c: Writing one byte forces copying an entire two-megabyte page
questions.d: They prevent multithreaded programs from ever calling mmap on a file
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write granularity follows page size, so fork plus a small write becomes a large memcpy. Option A overstates it: huge anonymous pages can still be swapped out.

questions.text: What does locking a memory region (mlock) do?
questions.a: Marks pages read-only so that writes trigger a fault
questions.b: Pins them so the reclaim code cannot evict them
questions.c: Reserves swap space for the entire address space
questions.d: Freezes the page table against any later kernel change
questions.explanation: Pinned pages stay resident, which is what key material and hard real-time loops need. Option A describes write-protect for copy-on-write, an unrelated mechanism.

questions.text: On a single-core machine, a thread spins on a lock whose holder was preempted. What follows?
questions.a: Its compare-and-swap fails and it gives up the loop
questions.b: The kernel quietly converts the spinlock into a mutex
questions.c: The preempted holder releases the lock during the switch
questions.d: The spinner burns the CPU the holder needs to finish
questions.explanation: Progress is blocked precisely because the waiter monopolises the only core. Option C confuses spinlocks with sleeping mutexes that support priority inheritance.

questions.text: What does the Linux load average actually count?
questions.a: Runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep
questions.b: Only the tasks that are executing on a core at this instant
questions.c: The percentage of CPU time spent in user code
questions.d: Processes queued for a container restart
questions.explanation: Disk-stalled tasks in D state raise it, so a high load can mean slow storage rather than busy CPUs. Option B is the natural but incomplete reading of the number.

questions.text: What is write amplification on a flash device?
questions.a: The filesystem splitting a single file across several extents on disk
questions.b: The page cache flushing the same dirty page twice
questions.c: Small random overwrites forcing whole erase blocks to be rewritten
questions.d: The I/O scheduler merging requests into larger ones
questions.explanation: The translation layer must copy valid pages and erase block-sized units, so host writes exceed logical writes. Option D is the opposite effect, which reduces work per byte.

questions.text: Which description matches the convoy effect?
questions.a: Threads migrating between cores as a group under load
questions.b: A long critical section queues waiters that then serialise behind each other
questions.c: A frequently written cache line ping-ponging between two cores' private caches
questions.d: The background writer reclaiming pages in a large batch
questions.explanation: Each released batch blocks the next arrivals, producing stair-step throughput. Option C is coherence traffic, a real effect but a different one.

questions.text: Why must a condition-variable wait be wrapped in a loop that re-tests a predicate?
questions.a: The mutex object is destroyed while other threads are still waiting on it
questions.b: Because wait returns only after an explicit timeout
questions.c: Because every signal is delivered as a broadcast
questions.d: Because wake-ups can be spurious and another thread may take the state
questions.explanation: Between signalling and rescheduling, the resource can already be consumed by a sibling waiter. Option C is wrong because a one-to-one signal exists, though it is easy to misuse.

questions.text: What does a readers-writer lock allow?
questions.a: Exactly one reader and one writer executing at the same instant
questions.b: Many concurrent readers, with writers getting exclusive access
questions.c: Unlimited writers as long as no reader is active
questions.d: Readers writing while still holding the shared lock
questions.explanation: Shared read access trades against an exclusive write phase, which is where writer starvation comes from. Option D would break the invariant the lock exists to protect.

questions.text: Why can a lock-free structure using relaxed atomics pass on x86 and break on ARM?
questions.a: x86 orders memory strongly; ARM reorders loads and stores more
questions.b: ARM processors simply have no compare-and-swap instructions available at all
questions.c: Relaxed operations are undefined behaviour in the language
questions.d: x86 cache coherence makes torn writes impossible anywhere
questions.explanation: Publication needs acquire and release or a fence, which x86 largely provides by default. Option B is false; the instruction set provides atomic primitives, just weaker ordering.

questions.text: What does opening a file with O_DIRECT ask the kernel to do?
questions.a: Cache the whole file until the process exits
questions.b: Round every write up to a page multiple and require aligned user buffers
questions.c: Bypass the page cache and move data between user buffers and the device
questions.d: Serialise writes so the device cannot reorder them
questions.explanation: The application takes over caching, losing readahead and sharing in exchange for control. Option B is half-true, since alignment is required, but it is a constraint rather than the purpose.

questions.text: A container is killed by the out-of-memory killer although its resident set stayed under its limit. What is the likely story?
questions.a: The scheduler preempted it during a page fault window
questions.b: A full filesystem makes every allocation call return an error immediately
questions.c: It asked for a huge page, which cgroups always refuse
questions.d: Overcommitted allocations were promised before reclaim could find frames
questions.explanation: Memory is only really committed when touched, so reclaim can fail even under a nominal limit. Option B produces write errors instead, not a kernel-selected SIGKILL.

questions.text: What is the practical difference between syncing a file and syncing its parent directory?
questions.a: They are the same call with arguments in another order
questions.b: The directory sync makes the new or renamed entry itself durable
questions.c: Syncing one file always flushes every other dirty file on the same device
questions.d: The directory sync only exists on journaling filesystems
questions.explanation: A rename's durability lives in the directory's data, which the file's own sync never touches. Option D mistakes a general filesystem property for a journal-specific feature.

questions.text: What does a thread's stack hold that the process heap does not?
questions.a: Globals shared by all threads of the program
questions.b: Library text mapped into the process by the dynamic linker at startup
questions.c: Frames with locals and return addresses for that thread
questions.d: Socket descriptors owned by that thread alone
questions.explanation: Each thread gets a private call chain and register spill area above a shared data section. Option D is the usual misconception: descriptor tables belong to the process.

questions.text: Which statement about priority inversion is accurate?
questions.a: It occurs when two equal-priority threads are run round-robin
questions.b: It is cured by simply giving every thread the highest available priority
questions.c: It can only happen where scheduling is not preemptive
questions.d: Priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder's priority
questions.explanation: The holder runs at the highest waiting priority so it finishes and releases quickly. Option B destroys the ordering that made the deadline guarantee meaningful in the first place.

questions.text: What is the effect of mounting a busy log volume with noatime?
questions.a: Fewer metadata writes, since reads no longer dirty the inode
questions.b: Reads skip the page cache and always reach the device
questions.c: Files become immutable until the filesystem is remounted
questions.d: The journal is disabled, so recovery needs a full filesystem check
questions.explanation: Access times are pure bookkeeping, and suppressing them removes a hidden write per read. Option B confuses it with direct I/O, which is a per-file flag rather than a mount option.

questions.text: A child process has exited but still shows in the process table. What is it?
questions.a: A zombie, awaiting reaping by its parent
questions.b: A stopped process suspended by a signal
questions.c: An orphan adopted by the init process
questions.d: A daemon detached from its controlling terminal
questions.explanation: Only the exit status remains, held until the parent calls wait; an orphan is reparented and eventually reaped, so option C is the usual confusion.
